stem: A `search_orders` tool executes successfully and returns zero matching orders. How should the agent treat this?

options.label: A
options.body: Accept it as a valid empty result — the absence of data is the answer.
options.rationale: Correct. The tool ran successfully; zero results is a legitimate outcome, not an error. 'Not found' is deliberately not an error category.

options.label: B
options.body: Treat the zero-result search as an error condition and retry the call in case the empty response was a transient failure.
options.rationale: Retrying a successful empty search just repeats a valid result — nothing failed.

options.label: C
options.body: Return isError=true so the model knows something went wrong.
options.rationale: Marking a valid empty result as an error misleads the model into thinking the tool failed.

options.label: D
options.body: Escalate to a human because no data was found.
options.rationale: An empty result doesn't warrant escalation; it's simply the answer.

stem: Which of these is an access failure that warrants retry/escalation rather than a valid empty result?

options.label: A
options.body: The API returns 401 Unauthorized.
options.rationale: Correct. A 401 (or a network timeout, or a 429 rate limit) means the tool failed to execute — retry with correct credentials or escalate.

options.label: B
options.body: A database query returns an empty set.
options.rationale: That's a valid empty result — the record simply doesn't exist.

options.label: C
options.body: A filter matches no items.
options.rationale: Valid empty — refine the filter or report no matches; nothing failed.

options.label: D
options.body: A search returns 0 results.
options.rationale: Valid empty — the absence of data is the answer.

stem: In MCP's architecture, how do two MCP servers exchange information?

options.label: A
options.body: They don't connect directly — all communication routes through the client/host.
options.rationale: Correct. MCP is a three-layer model (Host ⊃ Client ↔ Server). Servers expose tools/resources; the client connects to servers and routes calls. Servers don't talk to each other.

options.label: B
options.body: Servers open direct peer-to-peer connections to each other.
options.rationale: MCP servers don't connect directly — that's a classic distractor.

options.label: C
options.body: Through a shared database that both MCP servers read from and write to in order to pass information between them.
options.rationale: Not part of the MCP model; communication goes through the client/host.

options.label: D
options.body: Via a common event bus that the MCP servers publish messages to and subscribe from to exchange their information.
options.rationale: No event bus between servers; the client/host mediates.

stem: Your team needs a Postgres integration for Claude. What does the guide recommend before building a custom MCP server?

options.label: A
options.body: Check for an existing community MCP server first; only build custom when none meets your needs.
options.rationale: Correct. Use community servers first — building custom is the fallback for genuinely unmet requirements.

options.label: B
options.body: Always build a custom MCP server from scratch for the Postgres integration in order to get full control over exactly how it behaves.
options.rationale: Building custom for a common integration wastes effort when a community server exists.

options.label: C
options.body: Skip MCP entirely and have Claude call the Postgres database directly from within the prompt rather than through a tool interface.
options.rationale: That bypasses the tool interface entirely and isn't the recommended integration path.

options.label: D
options.body: Wait for Anthropic to ship an official Postgres MCP server before building any database integration for the team at all.
options.rationale: The guidance is to reuse community servers now, not wait.

stem: Claude keeps mis-selecting between similar tools. What is the correct FIRST optimization step?

options.label: A
options.body: Improve the tool descriptions; then add few-shot examples; consolidate tools only as a last resort.
options.rationale: Correct. The optimization sequence is descriptions → few-shot → consolidate. Descriptions are the primary selection signal, so start there.

options.label: B
options.body: Immediately reduce the number of tools available to the agent so there are fewer similar ones for it to confuse when selecting.
options.rationale: Reducing tools is the last step, not the first — fix descriptions before cutting tools.

options.label: C
options.body: Rename the similar tools to shorter names so the model has an easier time telling them apart from one another when it picks one.
options.rationale: Names aren't the primary selection signal; descriptions are.

options.label: D
options.body: Force a specific tool with tool_choice on every call so the model never has to choose between the similar tools itself.
options.rationale: Forcing one tool removes the model's judgment and isn't a general selection fix.

stem: You must always get structured output, but the incoming document could match one of several extraction schemas and you don't know which upfront. Which tool_choice setting?

options.label: A
options.body: tool_choice: "any" — guarantees a tool call while letting the model pick the right schema.
options.rationale: Correct. `any` forces some tool call (so you always get structured output) but lets the model choose which extraction tool fits the document.

options.label: B
options.body: Use a forced tool_choice pinned to one specific named extraction tool for every document, regardless of which schema it actually matches.
options.rationale: Forcing one tool assumes you know the single structure — you don't, since the document type is unknown.

options.label: C
options.body: Use tool_choice: "auto" and let the model decide whether to call an extraction tool at all or just reply with plain text instead.
options.rationale: `auto` lets the model reply with text and skip tools — no guarantee of structured output.

options.label: D
options.body: Rely on prompt-based JSON instructions asking the model to return the correct schema without any tool-level enforcement of the shape.
options.rationale: No schema enforcement — risks malformed or incomplete JSON.

stem: In a normal agentic loop where the model should decide when to call tools versus respond with text, what's the correct tool_choice default?

options.label: A
options.body: auto — the model decides whether to call a tool.
options.rationale: Correct. `auto` is the default for agentic loops; the model needs freedom to call tools or answer in text.

options.label: B
options.body: any — force the model to call some tool on every turn.
options.rationale: Forcing a tool every turn prevents the model from ever finishing with text — can cause loops.

options.label: C
options.body: A forced choice naming one specific tool to call.
options.rationale: Forcing one tool removes the model's judgment about when to act.

options.label: D
options.body: none — disable tool calling for the whole loop.
options.rationale: Disabling tools defeats the point of an agentic loop.

stem: You need to find every file whose name ends in `.config.ts` across a large repo. Which built-in tool is the most specific fit?

options.label: A
options.body: Glob — find files by name/path pattern.
options.rationale: Correct. Glob is for file discovery by name/extension patterns. Use the most specific tool for the job.

options.label: B
options.body: Grep — search file contents by pattern.
options.rationale: Grep searches inside files for content; here you're matching filenames, which is Glob's job.

options.label: C
options.body: Bash with a find command.
options.rationale: Avoid Bash for tasks a specialized tool handles better; Glob is the specific fit.

options.label: D
options.body: Read each file to check its name.
options.rationale: Read is for known file paths, not for discovering files by pattern.

stem: An MCP tool hits a downstream timeout. What should it return so the agent can respond intelligently?

options.label: A
options.body: Structured metadata: errorCategory "transient", isRetryable true, and a human-readable description.
options.rationale: Correct. A timeout is transient/retryable; structured metadata (category + retryable + description) lets the agent decide to retry rather than guess.

options.label: B
options.body: A generic "Operation failed" string with no category, no retryability flag, and no description of the cause for the agent to reason about.
options.rationale: A generic string gives the agent nothing to reason with — return structured metadata.

options.label: C
options.body: An empty but successful-looking result so that the agentic loop simply continues on past the timed-out call as if data had come back.
options.rationale: Empty-success hides a real failure and makes the agent think no data exists.

options.label: D
options.body: Throw an uncaught exception straight out of the tool handler so the failure surfaces however the surrounding runtime happens to handle it.
options.rationale: Uncaught exceptions break the tool protocol and give the model nothing to reason about.
